paras: The threatened lynching of William Dorsey at Peach Bottom took place in York County, Pennsylvania, on August 11, 1903, when a mob formed to lynch Dorsey and a second Black man after a fight at a hotel. The legal authorities jailed both men at York before the mob reached them, and Dorsey was later convicted of assault and sentenced to four years.

According to a York dispatch, Dorsey and a companion, printed as Charles Haywood in one paper and Charles Maywood in another, were refused drinks at John T. Moore's hotel. The dispatch called the two "desperate characters" who had been terrorizing the lower end of the county.

In the wire account, the men assaulted Moore with revolvers and knives, and Moore filled Dorsey's hip and back with shotgun fire. As news spread, the Alexandria Gazette's copy added, "a mob having been formed to administer lynch law"; the authorities captured the men and carried them to the York jail.

A York dispatch of August 31 reported that Dorsey and a Charles A. Forward, charged by Moore and two Maryland men with assault and battery with intent to kill and carrying concealed weapons, had been found guilty and each sentenced to four years in the Eastern penitentiary. No action against the mob appears in the coverage.

On August 13 the Alexandria Gazette ran the brief as "Lynchings Averted," and the Washington Times as "Negroes Denied Drinks Assault Hotel Man" over "Race Riot Near York, Pa., Narrowly Averted." Both called the fight "a small race war" and told it from Moore's side, giving the men's assault as fact. The Forest Republican presented the conviction as a "Quick Operation of Law," noting that Forward's case took under a day; no Black-press account appears in the coverage.

The trial report's Forward is probably, though not certainly, the Haywood or Maywood of the wire story. The wire said both men were jailed after the fight, while the later dispatch placed Forward's arrest on a Thursday just before his trial.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Dorsey at Peach Bottom
bases: A mob was reported formed 'to administer lynch law' against two Black men who were then jailed before it reached them, a threatened lynching rather than general intimidation (A1, A2).

The mob threat rests on one York wire dispatch printed in two papers (A1, A2); the later trial report (A3) independently confirms the fight with Moore and the prosecution of Dorsey but says nothing of a mob.

accounts.label: York wire report
accounts.gist: Two Black men denied drinks attacked Moore with revolvers and knives; he shot Dorsey, a mob formed, and authorities got both men to the York jail ahead of it.

accounts.label: York court report
accounts.gist: Forward and Dorsey, charged by Moore and two Maryland men, were tried and each sentenced to four years, Forward within a day of his arrest.

framing.detail: Both papers ran the York dispatch as a 'small race war' brought on by the men, calling them 'desperate characters' who had been 'terrorizing the lower end of the county', with the averted lynching as the headline.
The Forest Republican framed the conviction as a 'Quick Operation of Law', stressing that Forward's case took under 24 hours.
